Assamese.note: Assamese uses the Eastern Nagari script. ৰ and ৱ are especially important Assamese letters.

Bengali.note: Bengali is an abugida. Consonants take vowel signs; a hasanta suppresses the inherent vowel.

Bodo.note: Modern Bodo in India is commonly taught in Devanagari. The language's sound system is not identical to Hindi, so learn Bodo pronunciation separately.

Dogri.note: Modern Dogri education commonly uses Devanagari. Dogri is tonal; knowing the letters is only the first step.

Hindi.note: Hindi uses Devanagari. Also learn common nukta letters for Persian/Arabic loans.

Konkani.note: This beginner course uses Devanagari, the official script for Konkani in Goa. Konkani is also written in Roman, Kannada and Malayalam scripts in different communities.

Maithili.note: This beginner course uses modern Devanagari. Maithili also has the traditional Tirhuta/Mithilakshar script.

Marathi.note: Marathi uses Devanagari and commonly teaches extra vowel symbols such as ऍ and ऑ.

Nepali.note: Nepali uses Devanagari. Chandrabindu is important in words such as गाउँ.

Sanskrit.note: Sanskrit preserves the most complete traditional Devanagari vowel inventory. ॡ is extremely rare but shown for completeness.

Gujarati.note: Gujarati is an abugida related to Devanagari but without the continuous top headline.

Punjabi.note: Punjabi in India is normally written in Gurmukhi. The traditional core is the ਪੈਂਤੀ ਅੱਖਰੀ (35 letters), plus modern extended letters.

Odia.note: Odia is a rounded Brahmic abugida. Learn independent vowels first, then consonants and vowel signs.

Tamil.note: Tamil traditionally teaches 12 vowels (உயிர்), 18 consonants (மெய்), and the special āytham ஃ. Grantha-derived letters are used in many loanwords.

Telugu.note: Telugu is an abugida. A consonant such as క is normally read with an inherent vowel; vowel signs change it.

Kannada.note: Kannada is an abugida with independent vowels, consonants, dependent vowel signs and a virama.

Malayalam.note: Malayalam is a rounded abugida. It also has special chillu letters used for consonants without a following vowel.

Manipuri.note: Modern Manipuri/Meiteilon is taught in Meitei Mayek. The core letters are Eeyek Ipee; Lonsum letters are final-consonant forms.

Santali.note: Ol Chiki is an alphabet, not an abugida. It has 30 primary letters and its own digits.

Urdu.note: Urdu is written right-to-left. Letters join in different ways depending on their position. Short vowels are often shown only in teaching text.

Kashmiri.note: Kashmiri is written right-to-left and, unlike Urdu, normally marks its vowel system much more explicitly.

Sindhi.note: Sindhi's Perso-Arabic alphabet is unusually large because it writes implosive, aspirated and retroflex consonants distinctly. It is written right-to-left.
